prompt: Write a ~700-word professional workplace message about: proposing a change to the on-call rotation. Plain prose.
text:
Subject: Proposal for Optimization of Our Current On-Call Rotation Schedule

Team,

As we continue to navigate an increasingly complex technical landscape and respond to evolving user demands, I have been reviewing our current operational protocols with fresh eyes in recent weeks. Specifically, the existing on-call rotation has served us well since its inception; however, as our infrastructure scales and incident frequency shifts towards more specialized areas of the stack, certain inefficiencies within the schedule are beginning to impact both response times and overall team morale. It is therefore my recommendation that we pause for a brief moment to evaluate and propose specific changes to how we manage our duty roster moving forward.

The primary driver for this proposal stems from an analysis conducted over the last quarter regarding incident resolution metrics. While our Mean Time to Acknowledge (MTTA) remains within acceptable parameters, there has been a noticeable trend in increasing Mean Time to Resolve (MTTR) during specific shifts. This is not indicative of a lack of effort or skill among engineers on duty; rather, it points to structural issues with the current rotation design. Currently, our schedule relies heavily on rotating entire pods through generalist support duties regardless of their primary domain expertise at that moment. While this approach ensures coverage across all systems superficially, it often places highly specialized backend engineers in situations where they are forced to triage frontend or database issues for which they have less immediate familiarity with the current production state changes or architectural nuances introduced recently.

Consider a hypothetical scenario involving our migration project last month. During that week's rotation, two senior architects were placed on duty while their primary focus was leading the data layer migration. Simultaneously, junior developers handled legacy API queries. The result was a fragmented response capability where critical database locking issues faced longer resolution times than anticipated because the engineer on call lacked deep context regarding the specific migration scripts running in the background. By contrast, if we had aligned our rotation to match current project focus areas—placing backend specialists specifically when their respective domains are undergoing significant change—we could have likely mitigated these delays entirely without sacrificing coverage breadth.

The second critical factor necessitating this shift is the human element of sustainable engineering practice. The nature of on-call work involves a degree of cognitive load that extends beyond simply fixing bugs; it requires maintaining high-level situational awareness while often managing personal responsibilities after standard hours. Our current four-week rotating cycle results in unpredictable sleep disruption patterns for many team members, particularly those with non-standard family schedules or caregiving duties who struggle to predict their availability based on a fixed calendar rather than the nature of their work. This unpredictability contributes to burnout and can indirectly affect productivity even during off-hours when engineers are trying to rest after a grueling shift in an area outside their comfort zone.

Therefore, I propose we transition from a rigid temporal rotation model to a competency-based scheduling framework for specific critical systems. Under this new structure, high-risk or highly complex subsystems would maintain dedicated "specialist on-call" slots filled by engineers with proven expertise in those domains for defined periods (e.g., three months), followed by rotational coverage for standard maintenance tasks. For general infrastructure and low-complexity services, we can revert to the traditional rotating model as was previously effective. This hybrid approach ensures that when a major incident occurs regarding our most critical path features, it is handled immediately by someone who knows the code intimately rather than an engineer learning on the fly from documentation alone.

Implementing this change will require some upfront planning and perhaps a temporary adjustment to how we staff meetings or release cycles during transition periods. We must also establish clear protocols for handoffs between specialist shifts and rotational shifts to ensure seamless continuity of knowledge transfer. However, the long-term benefits regarding reduced incident duration, lower stress levels within the team, and improved retention rates make this investment essential.

I would like to schedule a dedicated workshop next week where we can discuss these points in detail, refine the proposed hybrid model, and address any concerns related to coverage gaps or resource allocation. My goal is not merely to change the calendar but to build a more resilient organization that supports its people as much as it protects our services. Thank you for your time and consideration of this important initiative.

Best regards,

[Your Name]
[Your Title]
